title: Minnesota lawyer suspended over fake AI case citations

reading.body:
A lawyer used an AI system to generate legal citations for a court filing without verifying them against actual case law. Two of the cases cited did not exist, and a third citation included a false quotation. The opposing party discovered the fabrication and brought it to the court's attention, revealing a failure to apply basic professional diligence before submission to a judge.

This shows what happens when an AI system's output, which can assert nonexistent facts with confidence, enters a professional workflow without human verification at the point of use. The lawyer had access to the tools needed to check citations, but did not use them. The failure occurred in the critical step between AI generation and court filing, where a competent review would have caught all errors.

It is not established whether the lawyer knew the citations were false or relied on the AI system's assertions without checking.

reports.title: Minnesota lawyer suspended over fake AI case citations

summary:
Minnesota attorney Faisal S. Ahmed was suspended for submitting fake legal case citations generated by artificial intelligence in a court filing. Ahmed cited two nonexistent cases, Anderson v. City of Biwabik and Doherty v. Alma E. Clark Memorial Home, in a 2025 memorandum filed in Hennepin County Court to support his client's position in a civil dispute. The opposing attorney discovered the fabricated citations and alerted the judge. Ahmed also included a false quotation from a real case and made additional citation errors in the brief.

Judge Lois Conroy ruled against Ahmed's client and ordered defendants to pay $233,563 in back rent. She fined Ahmed $5,000 and referred him to the Minnesota Lawyer's Professional Responsibility Board. Ahmed subsequently agreed to a 30-day suspension of his law license and to pay an additional $900 in costs. The judge emphasized that artificial intelligence tools should not replace proper legal analysis, noting that over 800 documented instances of AI-generated fake legal citations have been catalogued.
